newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Risky repairs delayed to struggling Mir station.
newsitem.headline: Risky repairs delayed to struggling Mir station.

text.p: Risky and difficult repairs to the Mir space station were postponed as the Russian-American crew and mission control struggled on Friday to right a navigational problem before the arrival of a vital supply craft.

Underlining the complexity of the cosmonauts' preparations for restoring electric power from a module holed last week, flight director Vladimir Solovyov said the crew needed an extra week to get ready after originally planning the job for July 11.
"This is a rather complicated job," he told reporters at Mission Control near Moscow. "That is why the sortie into the Spektr (module) is put off to July 17 or 18."
The crew and cosmonauts on the ground are working out manoeuvres by which power cables in the airless and cramped Spektr module can be reattached while wearing clumsy spacesuits.

Adding to difficulties on Mir, where electric power was cut by up to half by the collision with an unmanned cargo vessel on June 25, mission control was still struggling to restore a steering mechanism which keeps Mir's remaining solar panels lined up to the Sun in order to gain maximum power.
Solovyov said he hoped the malfunction of the "gyrodine" devices would be fixed by the time a new Progress cargo ship blasts off on Saturday at 0411 GMT carrying supplies needed for the repair work.
But he conceded that engineers were still looking for the cause of the problem, which has affected Mir more than once since the accident during a practice docking manoeuvre.
"We expect that by the time Progress is launched we will be able to cope with the gyrodines' problem," Solovyov said.
"We are about to find the reason, but at this very moment it has not been found," he said.
In the absence of the gyrodines, the three-man crew have had to keep Mir lined up with the Sun by firing their rocket motors, consuming fuel.

Russian space officials have warned that the loss of power on the station will make docking with the supply craft difficult. But Solovyov said the operation, due to take place on Monday, was not threatened by the gyrodine malfunction.

Asked about the risks commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin face during their venture into the airless Spektr module, Solovyov said: "The sortie to Spektr is no more dangerous that a space walk. We're not going to send the cosmonauts like lambs to the slaughter."
He repeated that British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale will don a rescue spacesuit during the repair operation and direct his Russian colleagues via intercom from Mir's Soyuz escape capsule.

"After the collision the cosmonauts felt pretty low," Solovyov said. "But now they are rather energetic, they have a good appetite, they work a lot -- even more than is needed -- and are perfectly aware that the trip into Spektr is a must."
